title: The Box Model
summary: The browser lays out each element as a box with content, padding, border, and margin.

subtopics.title: Content
subtopics.explanation: Content is the text, image, or child material inside an element. A declared width often applies to this area under the default content-box model. It is like the picture inside a frame. Content can grow, so check long labels and translated text rather than assuming it always fits. For example, a content width of 200px becomes wider after padding is added in content-box mode.

subtopics.title: Padding
subtopics.explanation: Padding is space between the content and the border. It gives text and controls room to breathe. It is like the mat around a picture. Padding is part of the clickable area for many controls, so it can improve usability as well as appearance. For example, padding can make a small button easier to activate without changing its text.

subtopics.title: Border
subtopics.explanation: The border is the visible edge around the padding and content. It can show grouping, focus, or an input boundary. It is like the frame around a picture. Include its thickness when measuring layout, and keep keyboard focus outlines visible even if the design changes other borders. For example, a visible border takes space and can affect the final outside measurement.

subtopics.title: Margin
subtopics.explanation: Margin is space outside the border that separates one box from neighboring boxes. It is like the gap between framed pictures on a wall. Margins can collapse in some block layouts, which surprises beginners. Use layout tools such as Grid or Flexbox when spacing between a group of items should be consistent. For example, adjacent margins can collapse in some block layouts, so inspect the resulting gap.

subtopics.title: Total width
subtopics.explanation: `box-sizing: border-box` makes the declared width include content, padding, and border. It is like measuring the entire framed picture instead of only the image. This makes responsive sizing easier to predict. Many projects apply it to all elements as a consistent baseline. For example, with border-box, a declared width includes padding and border for easier sizing.

foundations.overview: Every HTML element is laid out as a box with content, padding, border, and margin. These layers affect the space an element uses and the distance between neighbors. Think of a framed picture: the image is content, the mat is padding, the frame is border, and the wall gap is margin. `box-sizing: border-box` makes declared sizes easier to reason about.
foundations.whyItMatters: The box model explains why elements are larger or farther apart than their width declarations suggest. Understanding its layers makes responsive sizing and alignment easier to debug.
foundations.browserPerspective: During the layout (reflow) stage, the browser computes each box's content size, then adds padding and border (per box-sizing) to get the border box, and finally reserves margin space when positioning the box relative to its siblings and parent.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Buttons (padding for tap targets), cards (padding + border + margin), centered containers (margin: 0 auto + max-width), and spacing systems all depend directly on the box model.
foundations.businessImpact: Predictable spacing and sizing produce polished, consistent UIs that build trust; box-model bugs cause misaligned, broken-looking pages that hurt credibility and conversion.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing the box model removes guesswork, so developers write spacing and sizing that stays correct as content and viewport change.
foundations.performanceImpact: The box model itself is cheap, but frequent changes to box dimensions (width, padding, margin) trigger reflow; batching style changes and avoiding layout thrashing keeps rendering smooth.
commonUseCases: Adding comfortable padding to buttons and inputs
Spacing cards and sections apart with margin
Centering a fixed-width container with margin: 0 auto
Applying box-sizing: border-box for predictable widths

commonMisconceptions.myth: Setting width: 200px always makes the box 200px wide.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Under the default content-box, padding and border are added on top, so the rendered box is wider. Use box-sizing: border-box to make width include them.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Vertical margins of 20px and 20px between two blocks add up to 40px.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Adjacent vertical margins collapse to the larger of the two (20px), not their sum.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Background color fills the margin too.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Backgrounds fill the content, padding, and border areas — the margin is always transparent.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Margin is part of the visible box background.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Margin sits outside the border and separates neighboring boxes.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A declared width always equals the outside width.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Under content-box, padding and border add to the declared content width.

visualExplorer.title: Interactive box model
visualExplorer.caption: Adjust content, padding, border, and margin to see how each layer changes the element's total size.

interactiveExamples.title: See the four layers
interactiveExamples.explanation: A visible border and a colored background reveal where padding (inside) and margin (outside) sit.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Two blue boxes; the blue background fills content + padding, the border wraps it, and visible gaps (margins) separate them from each other and the gray page.

interactiveExamples.title: content-box vs border-box
interactiveExamples.explanation: Both boxes set width: 200px, but border-box keeps the rendered width at 200px while content-box grows wider once padding and border are added.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The content-box element renders 248px wide (200 + 40 padding + 8 border); the border-box element stays exactly 200px wide.

codeLab.title: Make a tidy card
codeLab.instructions: Style .card so it has comfortable inner padding, a subtle border with rounded corners, space below it, and a predictable width of 320px (padding and border must NOT make it wider). Hint: use box-sizing: border-box.

keyTakeaways: Content is the text, image, or child material inside an element.
Padding is space between the content and the border.
The border is the visible edge around the padding and content.
Margin is space outside the border that separates one box from neighboring boxes.
`box-sizing: border-box` makes the declared width include content, padding, and border.
